teaching.task: # HMS Year 12 V20 (Training for improved performance): classifying and assessing sports injuries. How are sports injuries classified, and how does TOTAPS decide whether a player can go back on? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Injuries are classified three ways, and every injury gets all three at once. Cause: a direct injury comes from an outside force, like a collision or a blow. An indirect injury comes from forces inside the body, like a hamstring tearing while sprinting. Cause tells you what might prevent it. Tissue: soft tissue is muscle, tendon, ligament and skin. Hard tissue is bone, including fractures and dislocations. Tissue tells you how urgent it is. And onset: an acute injury happens at one moment. An overuse injury builds up from repeated loading without enough recovery. Onset tells you where the real cause lies. Some books list overuse as a third cause instead. Either way, say it built up over time. Now the hook. The tackled shoulder is direct, possibly hard tissue, and acute, so stop and refer. The knee is indirect, likely a ligament, and acute. And the shin is indirect and overuse, so the problem is in the training, not just the leg. Precise names matter. A sprain is a ligament injury, a joint forced past its normal range, like rolling an ankle. A strain is a muscle or tendon injury, from an overloaded or poorly controlled contraction or stretch, often at speed or when tired. Sprain is ligament, strain is muscle or tendon. One letter apart, and marks are lost every year. A fracture is a broken bone. It may be obvious, or not, so persistent pain over a bone needs checking. A dislocation forces a bone out of its joint, often at the shoulder or a finger, with visible deformity. Never try to put it back. And remember, direct and indirect describe the cause, not how serious it is. A non-contact knee injury can be far worse than a knock.

scenes.teachingReason: Injuries are classified three ways, and every injury gets all three at once. Cause: a direct injury comes from an outside force, like a collision or a blow. An indirect injury comes from forces inside the body, like a hamstring tearing while sprinting. Cause tells you what might prevent it. Tissue: soft tissue is muscle, tendon, ligament and skin. Hard tissue is bone, including fractures and dislocations. Tissue tells you how urgent it is. And onset: an acute injury happens at one moment. An overuse injury builds up from repeated loading without enough recovery. Onset tells you where the real cause lies. Some books list overuse as a third cause instead. Either way, say it built up over time.

scenes.teachingReason: Precise names matter. A sprain is a ligament injury, a joint forced past its normal range, like rolling an ankle. A strain is a muscle or tendon injury, from an overloaded or poorly controlled contraction or stretch, often at speed or when tired. Sprain is ligament, strain is muscle or tendon. One letter apart, and marks are lost every year. A fracture is a broken bone. It may be obvious, or not, so persistent pain over a bone needs checking. A dislocation forces a bone out of its joint, often at the shoulder or a finger, with visible deformity. Never try to put it back. And remember, direct and indirect describe the cause, not how serious it is. A non-contact knee injury can be far worse than a knock.

scenes.teachingReason: TOTAPS is an on-field check for deciding whether an injured player can go back on. Its order is the point: each step asks a bit more than the last, so a serious injury is found before it's made worse. Talk: ask what happened, where it hurts, what they felt or heard. That gives the mechanism, and shows if they're alert. Observe: look at the area and compare it with the other side, for swelling or deformity. Touch: press gently, starting away from the pain and moving toward it, feeling for tenderness, heat, or pain right over a bone. Active movement: the player moves the joint themselves. Passive movement: you move it gently for them, through its range. And Skill: progressively harder movements, stand, walk, jog, run, change direction, then the actual skill. At any step, if it fails, stop. They don't go back on. Stopping early is a correct result, not a failed test.

scenes.teachingReason: Two things TOTAPS is not. It's not a diagnosis. It doesn't tell you which structure is damaged. Only qualified assessment can. And it's not for a suspected head, neck or spinal injury, or an unconscious player. Then you use the first aid steps from Year 11, don't move them, and call for medical help. Some calls are still judgement. A player gets through every step with mild pain throughout and wants to keep going. At school or club level, with no medical staff to recheck them, they don't return. A player insists they're fine and the game matters. Duty of care doesn't bend to what the player wants. And any suspected concussion, a brain injury from a knock to the head or a jolt through the body: no return that day, and medical clearance before playing again. If in doubt, sit them out.
